analysis.one_liner: Eliminates the federal agency that enforces firearms and explosives laws.
analysis.headline: A one-sentence bill to abolish the ATF drew 10 Republican cosponsors but never received a hearing or a vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have abolished the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) — the federal agency that licenses firearms dealers, traces guns used in crimes, licenses and inspects the explosives industry, and investigates arson and firearms trafficking. The bill text is one sentence with no plan for moving ATF's functions elsewhere. It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: The firearms industry and firearms dealers, who would face no federal licensing or inspections, no dealer compliance checks, and no federal tracing of crime guns. Others who chafe at federal firearms regulation would also gain, since the agency charged with enforcing federal gun laws would simply cease to exist.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gun dealers and the firearms industry

how_it_helps.text: Abolishes the ATF outright, ending its role licensing firearms dealers, tracing guns used in crimes, and investigating firearms trafficking and arson.
Removes federal oversight and inspection of the firearms industry with no replacement agency or transfer of functions in the bill.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people bear the cost: communities affected by gun trafficking and violent crime lose the agency that traces crime guns and investigates illegal gun sales, and the public loses the licensing and inspection regime for firearms and commercial explosives.

drawbacks.text: The bill abolishes the ATF with a single sentence and makes no provision for moving its functions — dealer licensing, explosives permits, crime-gun tracing — to another agency, leaving federal firearms and explosives laws without an enforcer.
Ending federal licensing and inspections of firearms dealers would remove the main check on straw purchases and illegal gun sales that supply traffickers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains flow to a specific industry: less federal licensing, inspection, and enforcement of gun sales. The costs are spread across the public, which loses the federal apparatus for tracing crime guns, policing illegal dealer conduct, and overseeing commercial explosives. Even supporters of reducing federal firearms regulation would have to acknowledge the bill offered nothing in place of the agency it erased.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced and sat there, with no hearing, markup, or vote, until the Congress ended two years later.

narrative.text: Rep. Matt Gaetz (R-FL) introduced the bill on January 17, 2023, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
The bill drew 10 Republican cosponsors in the House.
In nearly two years, the House Judiciary Committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.
On December 5, 2024, near the end of the Congress, Rep. Eric Burlison (R-MO) took over first sponsorship of the bill so cosponsors could be added, but the bill still never advanced.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal firearms and explosives enforcement continued unchanged, so the communities and the public-safety functions that depend on the ATF were better off that the bill died. The firearms industry, conversely, did not get the deregulation it would have gained from the bill's passage.

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, which sat at the referral stage for the entire 118th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 10 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the Republican-led House Judiciary Committee was the body that let the bill die without action.

industries.note: Abolishing the ATF would have ended federal licensing, compliance inspections, and crime-gun tracing that constrain gun dealers. The industry's gain would come from the public losing the enforcement regime for illegal gun sales.

ATF licenses and inspects explosives users such as demolition and mining firms. Abolition would lift oversight but also leave the industry without a federal licensing authority, creating uncertainty for lawful operations.
